title: the entry list
narrativeQuestion: How was the fastest sprinter in the world kept out of races when no rule said he could not race?

chapters.title: The boom
chapters.claim: The safety bicycle made riding possible for millions and the cycling lobby pushed for paved roads.

chapters.title: The sport
chapters.claim: Board track racing was a major paid spectator sport tied to bicycle sales.

chapters.title: The membership clause
chapters.claim: The 1894 League clause governed membership, and separate decisions by many actors kept Taylor out of races.

chapters.title: On the track
chapters.claim: Taylor was boxed in and assaulted, and his attacker at Taunton was fined fifty dollars.

chapters.title: World champion
chapters.claim: Taylor won the world sprint title at Montreal in 1899, five years after the clause.

chapters.title: The Sunday problem
chapters.claim: Taylor refused Sunday races, a cost he chose, which the standings cannot tell apart from refusals.

chapters.title: Europe
chapters.claim: The same rider met different decisions in Europe and won most of his match races.

chapters.title: The boom broke
chapters.claim: The industry consolidated and the sport lost its place.

chapters.title: How it ended
chapters.claim: Taylor died in 1932 in an unmarked grave and former riders marked it in 1948.
